COMMUNICATION. Another Turn to the Screw. The custom house in this Island, as long back as can be remembered, lias always predicated the export duty charged on Rum upon an average gauge of 105 gallons for each puncheon, a custom which was founded no doubt on correct data and well ascertained justice ; and its long continuance shows that it was approved by the Government here as well as in Denmark. It is well known to the simplest child in tlio country that our ltuin is nearly all, as a general rule, exported in Corn Meal puncheons, which range from þÿ103 110 gls. þÿ some may gauge as high as 111 þÿ 112 gls hut very seldom. Taking the average gauge therefore between þÿ103 110 gls., and making a fair and equitable allowance for wastage or outs, we feel convinced that this long sanctioned rule, will be considered no more than barely just by all unbiased persons who understand the matter at all Wlien a large crop happens to be made which unfortunately is rare) and Corn Meal puncheons become insufficient for the wants of the country, some planters may occasionally >et up a few þÿcreole puncheons (as they, are ernied) which may average somewhat more ban Corn Meal casks, but these exceptions are so insignificant that no Inspector of the Customs hitherto has ever thought it worthy of notice, or considered it a sufficient grotiml to authorise him to disturb a rule which must have originally been established upon proper consideration and mutual compact, and circumstances are certainly in no wise different now, in

consequence of hearing that our now Inspector has increased the standard gauge of Runt to 110 gls. per puncheon, how far he may be authorised I respect for the þÿ without the express orders of Government to alter a custom which lias so long existed, we know not. To our view the whole thing is but a pitiful, paltry cheese-paring affair, either i the Communication of þÿ as regards any increase of revenue it can produce to the Treasury, or the loss it may occa-

S T , C R 0 | X A v I S . sion to the producer or exporter. But it looks, we must confess, like a disposition to grind, which might perhaps better suit the meridian of West End. We regret it the more because we learn from some of the few who are acquainted with our Inspector that he appears to be a good Gentlemanly person, and we can only express our sorrow that he should consider it right to make himself known to us by a small affair like this, and we trust on further consideration his better judgment will prevail and that he will permit the old arrangement to continue. He is a stranger amongst us and is therefore entitled to our most favorable consideration þÿ although he may have been unfavorably impressed towards us þÿ we would accordingly suggest to him in a kindly spirit the prudence of forbearing from all alterations in old and recognized customs until at least time allows him to become a little better acquainted with circumstances and characters (we speak advisedly) that he may be better able to judge for himself, and in the meantime we would take the liberty to recommend him to receive with due caution the reports and suggestions which officious or designing persons may have made, or may make, to him for their own sinister purposes. The circumstances of the times and the declining condition of our trade ought to suggest a wiser and more liberal policy on the part of Custom-house officials than adding new restric" tions and impediments to a trade already overhardened with them, which in many instances

arc but mere senseless petty annoyances, after all, without even the merit of the smallest utility and apparently designed for effect, or to confirm the old adage, that, þÿ anew Broom sweeps þÿclean, or, in other words, when a new official is appointed to an office it generally seems that he gives all the trouble he can to the public in order to prove how much more vigilant lie is than Lis predecessors. Intelligently considered it mus1 appear much more requisite to slacken than to tighten the screw, both for the encouragement of Trade, as well as for the interest of the Treasury ; for, as a natural consequence, when the pressure is too severe means will he found to endeavour to evade it. We have been favoured by the Stewards of the St. Croix Races with the follo wing notes of the results of this, we may say, annual and only public amusement. The usual accommodations were provided by the Stewards as on previous occasions, but we regret to add that although every one seemed to participate in the amusements provided for the occasion, comparatively few seemed to consider it a duty to contribute their quota, however small, to defray the many expenses which must be connected with the preparations generally made. The Stewards, we learn, on each occasion, are put to considerable expense in the erection of an enclosure where the respectable our opinion, to justify the proposed alteration, j portion of the community may assemble We are induced to make these remarks in ' and be free from the disagreeable pressure experienced outside, but we regret to add that very few availed themselves of the accommodation, whether from too great a almighty þÿdollar or not we are unable to say.
In reference to the subject treated of in þÿCandour, we have heard that many years ago there existed a dispute between the Custom-House

Officers at West End, regarding the average guage of a puncheon of Rum, which, on befhg referred to the Government, was settled by determining the average guage at 105 gallons pr. puncheon. Some of our readers may perhaps be in a better condition to state the particulars of the occurrence.

From the St. Thomas Times, November 28. The contemplated Policy of Denmark in regard to the Sugar Duties. An extract from the St. Croix Avis, of the 24th instant, will tell our readers that

a meeting of Planters and Merchants was to have been held in that Island yesterday (the 27th), in order to consider course they a fluences which the muv pursue to counteract the injurious in- contemplated will Free- Trade policy their only Staple. of Denmark, It will be seen produce the from on said extract that a þÿCustom T s ariff is now or will be under discussion in the Diet in Copenhagen, and that one of the measures proposed is that ofremodeniug the differential or protective duty existing between foreign sugars and those of their own Colony. We cannot but admire the action of the Merchants and Planters in bestirring themselves in the hope of averting the intended blow, which, if only for the high state of cultivation St. Croix is at |ucscut in would like to see some resolution adopted calculated to throw it off'. But to our mind it. is that very inability to produce a counter-action that will make the efforts of the Colonists unavailing ; they have no retaliatory measure in their therefore that is left to them hands, and all will be to _ abide passively to the change, and, if protection is iiutispe usable, see their Instates gradually go into decay. It is. 'however, in cases like these that we behold the evils under which Colonies and Colonists labor, by being unable to provide for themselves against injurious legislation that State, for it often happens by the Parent that which is life to the one is death to the other. England, in removing by a gradual scale the

differential duties between her own Colonial Sugars and those of foreign places, made herself in great part by her capital the store-house of all Sugars destined to be consumed in Europe, as well as cheapening it at home. Denmark doubtlessly conceives that by remodelling her duties on Sugars she mav become the store-house for every particle of sugar destined to be consumed by all the nations whose seaports are within the Baltic; no doubt it is a sound policy as scruple regards herself, and St. she throws therefore with little Croix overboard. The scales, however, should at till times be made to balance, so that whilst Colonies exercise no influence in the Councils of an European State, no measure should be forced on a Colony that is objectionable to the ( lolonists. If such were the ease, and without stopping to point at any graver enactment, we should have need to shew but one little objectionable law recently passed upon us, so as to remove it, and that is The Local Postal Law!

Latest news from Gwalior to the 26th of September. Scindia had brought the mutineers of the Gwalior contingent under his control, by arraying against them his own troops and 10,000 tlmkoors, cutting off their supplies, &c. Division and dissension among the mutineers, who were asked for aid by a Shahzadah from Delhi on the one hand, and an emissary from the Nana on the other. A body of Ghorkas, 1,400 strong, under the command of Captain Bidden, attacked the insurgents at Mundree in the vicinity of feimgurgh on September 19. The enemy were defeated, and driven out of Mundree with a loss of 200.

Nothing new has occurred in Hajpootana. The Jodhpoor mutineers are still in force at Ajah. It is stated that they have extracted a large sum from the town of Palee as a ransom. A reinforcement is proceeding to join General Lawrence. The Malwa county is in a very disturbed state. The cantonment of Shopahwur has been burnt. Dbar, Arnjeera and Mundlaiser are disaffected. which otherwise would be open to attack from the Gwalior rebels. All lias remained quiet in Scinde since the dispatch of the last mail. CHRIST M A S-ALLOW A N C E . To the Editor of the Avis, Sir, Commune naufragmm dulct ! Having had to pay the new impost in the shape of Christmas Allowance to my labourers, it should, according to the sentence quoted above, be a sweet consolation, that this ruinous expense is now common for all Planters here. That consolation will nevertheless with mo sometimes become mixed with feelings of a very different kind when it occurs to me to argue within myself on j the matter ; and thus it has happened that the sweets of the common shipwreck have evaporated, ' and left me nothing but bitterness. This heavy annual cxpence is neither founded j in necessity, nor, of course, commanded by law, it being, on the contrary-, as much a de facto infringement of the Labour- Act, as the other bribes and overpayments so much complained of. it is, in fact, nothing but a reckless waste of money, introduced by some attorneys to absent proprietors, and, as the planters here are circumstanced, necessarily spreading over the whole Island like another plague. It comes ou an average to more than $100 for each Sugar-Estate, and that at times, when very few of them have been able from their revenues to defray their ordinary expcnces. But then, the Absentees are rich people, and some of their attorneys aspire to being leaders to the Planters. Had the expeuce to come out of the þÿattorney own s pocket, it may well be doubted whether he would have fancied leading in that direction There is something radically wrong in the mat-

ter. The very persons who first introduced the giving of Christmas Allowance, are ever ou the look-out, personally, aDd even by spies, for any overpayment ol wages, and cases of briberv, and having detected anything, are expeditious iu bringing the case before the Courts. Therein j they have the written law on their side, and they j mean to compel trespassers to conform thereto, j So far, so well. But, although no written law expressly forbids pi inters sharing several hundred dollarsas a presenqauiong their labourers, probably because no legislator could ever with all his wisdom foresee a system so full of folly, yet, there arc iu the case of the late Chamberlain þÿSobotker s moral obligations of no less force than written laws. While the wealthy proprietors seek to compel all others to obedience of the Regulations for payment of wages, hours of labour, and even labour by the time and not by task, in order that their owh labourers should have no such cause for dissatisfaction and eventually leave their Estates, they are themselves, in return, morally bound not to compel the less wealthy planters to either incur an expence they caunot afford, or cause disaffection among their labourers and thus ultimately bo ruined. But this they do by giving Christmas Allowance, thereby forcing their neighbors to the same, as it is notorious that no planter, whose ly comprehend why, or for whose bonefit, these neighbor gives it, would be able to escape the discontent of his labourers, and their giving him

notices in due time to quit his Estate, unless he 1 also consents to the impost. But, it is, at best, a tax imposed by the few upon the many against their will and without their being consulted, and therein lies the wrong of the few, although the law may not explicitly forbid their giving
May be their actions hope this, and let us further action alike honorable and prudent, and thus naufragium St. Croix, Christmas 1857. PLANTER.

The Wind of 'Projectiles. þÿ The fact that a cannon-ball passing close by a living subject exercises a Iatteral pressure on the air sufficient to produce a contusion has often been asserted, and as often denied. On this disputed matter M. E. Pelikan, of St. Petersburg, lias just presented a paper to the Academy of Sciences at Paris, giving an account of certain experiments instituted with a view to set the question at rest. Having obtained the concurrence of the Russian government, M. Pelikan caused a cylinder of sheet iron, one foot in diameter, to be constructed, with a piston moving easily inside. The piston-rod was provided at its outer extremity with a black lead pencil to mark the recoil on a slip of paper. The whole apparatus was firmly fixed on a strong wooden frame. The piston and pistourod weighed Sib., and a force of ljlb. was requisite to make the piston recoil an inch. At four m itres Jistance from the frame a wooden screen was erected, in order to ascertain the distance of the projectile from the piston at the moment of its passage. Although the experiment instituted iu 1843 and 1844 in the arsenal of Washington, by Major Mordicay proved that at the distance of 48 feet the gases emanating from the powder have no effect upon the balistic pendulum, a second screen was placed before the other at 5 þÿmetres distance from the apparatus, in order to protect it, if necessary from the action of these gases. A 40lb. howitzer was then placed at a distance of 14 metres from the first screen,

the charge of powder being 4lb.; the velocity of the projectile at that distance was equal to that of a bombshell projected with a 71b. charge þÿ viz., 956 feet per second. The results obtained showed, þÿ 1, thut at a distance of 3 inches, the piston remained immovable ; 2, that even when the projectile broke off a part of the wooden frame supporting the cylinder the piston gave no indication of motion ; 3, but that if the projectile just grazed the surface of the piston, a recoil of two inches was obtained ; 4, if, on the other hand, a fragment of the frame hit the cylinder the piston, instead of moving backwards, would move forwards about 3£ lines ; 5, if the cylinder, instead of being placed parellel to the screen, was placed obliquely, a recoil would take place of from one-quarter to one-half of an inch. Hence M. Pelikan concludes that since the piston required a force of I Jib. in order to be moved an inch, and the wind of a cannonball can never be expected to exercise such a force, the passage of a projectile close to a living subject will only produce an insignificant effect, which cannot amount to a contusion. þÿ London Times.

To the Young Ladies. þÿ I would speak tenderly to you, for, in many of your sex. lies, you are encouraged by the sterner fol- Yet there are some which are your own. Let me speak of two things þÿ extravagance and monstrosity in dress. In the days of your mothers, six or eight yards of silk was enough for a dress ; now you must have sixteen. This enormity does not beautify you ; it renders you hideous. There are some of your fashions which are so disgusting as hardly to be spoken ofþÿ I mean all those devices which have for their object the' swelling out of your forms, so as to give prominence to þÿ what shall I say ? As if to imitate the peacock, the very emblem of folly and vanity, you make your heads, the seat of the intellect, as little and insignificant as possible, while the hips are amplified into the dimensions of a balloon! This, my dear young ladies, is madness. In the first place, it is very inconvenient. With your hoops and crinoline, you are troublesome and annoying, especially in public places; in the street, in the church, the theatre, the omnibus and the rail ear. as they sweep up the mud and dust in the streets, and wipe the filth upon your pretty feet and ankles, are very irritating in crowded places, for they will be trod upon, and then you look daggers. And finally, my fair readers, these things, generated and encouraged by yourmantuamakers, and your fear of each other, disgust those whom you should desire to please; I mean young men. These modern extravagances of yours have done much to

degrade your sex in the eyes of our sex. 1 am an old man, and to me it is at once mournful and shocking to hear the vulgar, coarse jokes current among young gentlemen, founded upon your monstrous and extravagant fashions in dress. In the days when young ladies dressed and deported themselves modestly and tastefully these things were not so. I consider, therefore, that your vicious fashions have a positively vicious tendency in society þÿ they make you, thousands and hundreds of thousands of you, old maids ; and as many men thus made woman-scoffing old bachelors. In general, it may be said that Cupid never was found in padding or hoops. Men þÿdon f t all in love with walking store-cases. And, besides, these tomfooleries of yours are very costly ; and prudent young men, though they may waltz and polk with them, in general are very shy of marrying them. Is it not a good time to think of these things, and to correct the folly that they imply ? If I am a judge of the ways ol the world, I am sure that a return to the economy, delicacy, and good taste of other days, would greatly promote your happiness, as well as that of society in general, including your papas, who are. obliged to foot your bills.

A New þÿ TobaccoþÿQuestion. þÿ þÿ The blatant question ot the possibility of poisoning cigars impregnated with arsenic has been raised by the recent death, in France, of a priest named Bottaro, supposed to have been poisoned by another priest. An investigation lias been undertaken to ascertain whether it be possible or probable that arsenicuted cigars can cause death, | by the inspiration of their smoke, impregnated with volatilized arsenic, or by its admission in the saliva without such change ; aud very im- portant are the conclusions arrived at. þÿ There are four þÿways, remark the investigators, þÿ in which the introduction of arsenic into the animal economy may bo effected through the medium of cigars ; by impregnation with a powerful solution of the poison ; by its introduction into the candescent end, or as au impalpable powder into the buccal end, so that it may reach aud mix with the saliva during smoking, or, finally, in larger quantity, hidden in the central part of the cigar. Poisoning is hardly possible in the first or second cases. In the third distance it is inconceivable. It might occur by a combination of two or threo of these methods. The question of the formation of arseuiuretted hydrogen is not þÿsettled. In reading this report, we seem to be transported to the days of the Borgias, when the poisoned taper, falsely bearing the motto ullis iuserviendo conþÿsumer, destroyed other existences in sacrificing its own ; and when the flowers of the ball-room

wore scented with alien and lethal perfumes. It L well to be assured that these tabled horrors are also impossibilities. The mere suggestion of this most þÿ deleterious þÿsophistication of tobacco must carry alarm and discomfort to the soul of any rich uuclc in the habit of smoking bis favourite þÿnephew c s igars ; while for our modern ( blowers of anti-blasts to tobacco it furnishes a patent and effective insinuation. This report, however, practically negatives the possibility of such a crime being successfully perpetrated ; siuce it is only in those cases where the impalpable powder is made to mix with the saliva, in other words, where detection is almost inevitable, th it this detestable expedient could be effectively employed. þÿ The iMncet.

When the Atlantic telegraph-cable is once securely lodged on its shelf at the bottom of the sea, messages will be transmitted it from shore to shore of great oceanic basin, by causing a current of electricity to flow from one end to the other of the included copper strand, produce certain observable electrical effects upon its arrival. A suramount of ingenuity and skill lias been expended upon the preparation of the apparatus by which this result will be obtained. The primary source of the electrical power which will be employed in this service þÿ the fount whence the stream of electrical telegraphy will issue þÿ is a voltaic battery singular of excellence and gigantic power. There are first tea large cells of gutta-percha, strengthened outside by a wooden casing, and filled inside by a mixture of sulphuric acid and water. Into each of these cells project a number of lamina' or leaves. The laminae are composed of platinum-covered silver and mercuryamalgamated zinc alternately ; but all the are connected together beneath by long bar ; and all the silver leaves are connected together in a similar way by another bar above. Thus, all the silver element acts as one continuous plate, and all the zinc element does the same. Each metal exposes in one cell of the battery 2000 square inches of surface to be operated upon by the acid. The battery is thus composed, in electrical language, of ten pair of voltaic plates, each having 2000
inches of silver, and 2000 square | inches of zinc, exposed. The zinc and silver elements of each cell liavq been arranged in separate laminae, instead of in

So long as this process of renewal of the corrodible zinc plate is carried on, the giant battery will maintain itself continuously in unimpaired operation. About the end of August last Captain Berryman, in the U. S. Steamer Arctic, left H.ililax lor Bermuda, and proceeded with his dei p-sea soundings w ith uniform success until the loss of his entire sounding line, several thousand fathoms in length, put a stop to the experiments. Captain Berrymun's plan was to obtain soundings and thermal observations every thirty miles between Halifax and Bermuda, and from this place home. The experiments of Captain Berryinan, imperfect as they are, throw considerable light on the constitution and extent of the Gulf Stream. They have shewn that this Stream is comparatively a superficial current, and is underlaid by vast strata of water of a very low temperature. Specimens of the mud at the bottom corresponded with those obtained between Newfoundland and Ireland. The thermometer at timeR shewed that at a distance beneath the surface the mercury fell below zero. At the last sounding before the parting of the line and the loss of the apparatus the temperatures were much higher. The bottom was reached at three miles, and at that depth the thermometer stood at 25 degrees,

and gradually rose until at the surface it was 75 degrees. Between Halifax and Bermuda on the 10th October at 800 fathoms the thermometer recorded 2 degrees, at 500 fathoms 10 degrees, at 250 fathoms 15 degrees. TO Silt JAMES M ELY ILL, EAST INDIA HOUSE. Alexandria, Dec. 5, 1857. Intelligence from Bombay to the 17th Novemb.er: þÿ Sir Colin Campbell reached < 'awn poor on the 4th November, crossed the Ganges on the 9th, en route to Lucknow, with 5,000 men of all arms. General Windham commands the reserve at Cawnpoor. Colonel Grcathed's column arrived at Cawnpoor on the 25th of October, and proceeded on the 31st, under command of Brigadier Grant, being reinforced by 5,000 strong, with a large supply of provisions, to Allumbagh, where it awaits the arrival of the Commander-in-Chief. The Dinapoor mutineers were driven from a strong position at Binder near Futtehpoor, by a detachment of 500 men under Colonel Powell, 53rd Foot ; two guns captured, but with severe loss. Colonel Powell killed. '1 he accounts from Sangor and Jubbulpoor unsatisfactory. Major Erskine has earnestly demanded assistance. Brigadier Stuart's colmnu, on its route to Mhow, has been directed to proceed thither. I lie contingent at Mahedpoor mutinied on the 8th of November, and killed two of their officers; but a telegraphic dispatch, just received, states they were attacked by the Mhow field force, and routed, with loss of all their guns. Mhow and Indoor all quiet. the Rewah 1 hakoor and Rajpootana, muti- No further outbreaks in Joahpoor but neers are still in force. A reinforcement of 500 Infantry has proceeded from Gu/.erat to aid General Lawrence. All quiet in Bombay, with the exception of the Bheels in Khandeish, which are be-

ing put down. Phe Ghenghis Khan arrived at Bombay with a detachment of 3rd Dragoons and ltitli Foot. All quiet, in Scinde and the Punjab, as also in the Nizam's country. 1 >ates from < alrutta, direct to the 9th November; nothing of importance.

S; T , & ft 0 I a. V I ' The following telegram was received at the Foreigu-otlice, Dec. 11, 1857, at 5, 15 p.m. Alexandria, Dec. 5, 1857. The " Bombay" reached Suez on the 30th of Nov., bringing Bombay dates to the 17th of November. Greathed's column after the battle of Agra was pushing on with all haste towards Cawnpore, when on the 18th Brigadier Grant, of the 9th Lancers, joined and took command. On the 23rd they arrived at Kauouj, where the enemy was cut up by our cavalry, and five guns captured. The force, now about 3,500 strong, reached Cawnpore on the 26th, and being reinlorced to 5,000 crossed the Ganges on the 30th. They reached Alumbagh without obstruction on the 3rd, and there wait till the Commander-in-Chief joins them. Lucknow, said to be surrounded by 50,000 insurgents, had not been relieved at the date of the latest advices, but still held out. Our force at Alumbagh, only three miles from Lucknow, though in easy communication with Cawnpoor, had not received a line from Lucknow for more than a month. Heavy fighting, with slaughter, believed to have occurred. Sir Colin Campbell, who left Calcutta on the 27th of October, reached Cawnpoor on November 3, where he remained till the 9th, waiting, it is presumed, reinforcements which must bring up the force at Alumbagh, when he joins, to close on 10,000 men. On the 1st of November an action was fought near the village of Kudjnai, between the Diuapoor mutineers and a detachment of S00 men, consisting of part of the Naval Brigade and a detachment of the 93rd

Highlanders, with two nine-pounders, under Colonel Powell, of her Majesty's 53rd Foot. Our success was complete ; but loss heavy, Colonel Powell being among the killed The Naval Brigade afterwards fell back upon Binkee, with a view of returning to Futtepoor, and the rest of the troops reached Cawnpoor on the 2nd. The Rohilcund rebels had again advanced towards Nyneital and again taken to flight on linding that the little force from that place was approaching. Mehidpoor having been attacked on the 8th of November by a body of insurgent tribes from the neighbourhood, a portion of the Malwa Contingent joined the enemy, killed Captain Mills, Doctor Casey and Sergeants-Major O'Connell and Mansen, captured the guns and compelled the other troops to retire. According to latest accounts from Bombay, the 1st, 3rd and 4th divisions Nizam Cavalry, under Major Orr, attacked the rear-guard of the rebels on the 12th November at Barrarowah, recapturing the whole of the guns and stores taken, from Mehidpoor, also two of the enemy's guns ; 100 of the enemy killed, 74 prisoners. Our casualties not yet received, but said to be severe. The column under Brigadier Showers has captured Ahujjur, Dadree, Nunoond and other places S. W. of Delhi, securing upwards of .£70,000 worth of treasure. Further north, General Van Courtlaudt still keeps the country in order. The district between Agra and Meerut is so quiet that the post and passenger carriages run daily between the two places. Eastward of Oude the Nepaulese Contin-
gent has gained two victories over bodies of the insurgents. The steamer " Bengal" reached Suez on the 3rd instant from Calcutta, but brings no later dates than those from Bombay.
The dates from Hong Kong are to the 30th of October. Preparations were being made for the assault of Canton.

HAMBURG. Letters from Hamburg state that the Senate and the burgesses had come to an understanding. They have agreed to abandon the issue of a paper money and a forced circulation. A sum of 15,000,000, marcs banco (about 28,000,000, francs) will be granted to is the Treasury to deposit at the bank an amount bank of discount ; and the of 5,000,000, in shares of the railways from Berlin to Hamburg, and from Hamburg to Bergdorff, both being the property of the State. The bank will open with the Treasury an account current for these shares, and will begin to grant discounts to the extent of 5,000,000, marcs banco (equivalent to 9,000,000, francs). ' The State is, moreover, in negotiation abroad for 10,000, 000, marcs banco, in silver, to be also paid over to tlje Bank in the course of this week, and made applicable to the purposes of discount. Thursday, says A telegraphic þÿ : " communication dated Notwithstanding the the arrival of about 100,000,000, (francs) in silver, at Hamburg, during the past week þÿ notwithstanding the decisions of the Senate þÿyesterday failures have succeeded one another without intermission. The amount of bills of exchange protested since the commencement of the crisis is estimated at 140 to 150 millions. Yesterday the panic was at its height. Many hitherto strong houses were declared insolvent though possessed of considerable assets."

BELGllTM. The National Bank of Brussels has published its accounts up to the 30th of Novein her. From these it appears that in the midst of the general alarm at the pretended disappearance of precious metals, the metallic reserve of this bank has increased by 6,000,000 francs (£1240,000), >vhile the commercial paper in it has decreased by 4,000,000 francs ( £160,000). The circulation of notes has only increased by 2,300,- 000 francs ( £92,000).

ITALY. The official Gazzetta di Verona says that there is very great depression in Lombardy, of silk has fallen above 50 per cent., " and and a total stagnation of trade. The price things are likely to be still worse when this year's produce is brought into the market." Several houses suspended their payments on the 1st of December, and one of the first firms in Milan would also have been obliged to do so if it had not had most efficient assistance. During the last tew days there have been no bankruptcies here, but several firms have suffered severe losses during the present monetary and commercial crisis.

FRANCE Ferouk Khan, the Persian Envoy, has formally applied to the French Government for permission to engage French officers for instructing the army of the Shah. His request is likely to be accorded. Baron Pichon, the French Charge d'Affaires, now on his way to Teheran, has been received in Persia with marked distinction and respect.

The latest telegram from Trieste, dated at a quarterpast 9 on Friday morning, enables us to replace the article on Indian affairs, printed in our early edition, by the confirmation of most of its anticipations. All attention is still fixed on Lucknow; there the suspense of the contest rests Havelock has reinforced the garrison, and he and Sir J. Outram hold the Residency with some two thousand men, if so many survive from fighting their way through the city and from the subsequent suffering in the siege, while sixty or seventy thousand Sepoys and brigands, with 300 guns, hold their encampment around him. At the garden residence of Alumbagh, three miles off, there had been about 800 troops at the previous advices. The communication between Alurnbagh and the Residency was quite cut off by the overwhelming number of the rebels. Thus, from Outram and Havelock the direct accounts almost fail us. Their garrison is still the refuge of all the women and children originally harboured there, with the exception of such as have fallen victims to inevitable privation and sickness. Here the fresh intelligence takes up the story and justifies every hope that the bravest and the staunchest who have earned the fullest right to glory in the final triumph will not be denied the unequalled gratification of sharing in it. The Foreignoffice telegram tells us that Greathed's column achieved its wondrous march to Cawnpoor by the 25th, having won, as we had been previously informed, such successes on its way from Agra as would

at any other time have earned enthusiastic praise for those who gained them. But our heroes must be content for the moment that their lesser deeds should bo obscured by their own greater ones. Brigadier . Grant appears now to have taken the command of the column, and it is raised by reinforcements from 3,500 to an army of 5,000 men, in which number it reaches Aluinbagh. This strength would almost in itself have justified the Brigadier in at

once trying the fortune of war, and dashing forward to the effectual relief of the Residency at Lucknow, and the dispersion of its assailants. Here, however, there is a momentary pause, although the British garrison is reported to be short of provisions, killing its own draught oxen ; and the Grant and Greathed column bring ample supplies, as well as welcome reinforcements. The time is come for the Connnandea-in-Chief to appear in the field Sir Colin Campbell, it will be seen, reached Cawnpoor on the 4th November, crossed the J- 1 i -res on the 9th, doubtless with that formidable artillery train of which we had been before apprised, and which was to lay the streets in ruii.s from behind the walls of which the Sepoys had inflicted so much loss on Sir James Outram's division. Sir Colin had 5,090 men of all arms. He will in person fight the great decisive battle against the congregated remains of the Sepoy strength ; and, as iie lias S00 cavalry, he will not be obliged to allow them to run from the battle-field and escape by the mere nimbleness of their legs. With help so near them, it would be almost pusillanimous to fear that Generals Outrain and Havelock have not held out. A salute ol camion would apprise them, as they had apprised the besieged before, that the succour was on the spot, and that, after a weary interval, the joyful day of open battle had dawned. On this ground we have all along taught our readers to believo that the final blow must be struck which will bring the hopeless fall of the insurrec-

tion. Saugor, we are sorry to see, in spite of the boast of a recent private letter, is yet in danger, though here again Brigadier Stuart is within a few days' march to bring relief. The massacre at Hurrowtee has completed its evil work. Lieutenant Osborne is relieved at Rewali. Sir Colin Campbell has the opportunity, befitting his rank and fame, of crushing the revolt in its focus. The victory which awaits him closes the war. Bands of considerable number and ferocious with absolute despair, will yet prowl over the north central districts of India, even when the main force is dealt with by Sir Colin Campbell ; insecurity will be the curse of all well-disposed people, native and European. Bur the remaining work will become more and more au affair of police instead of a campaign between two disciplined armies.

RUSSIA. The Paris Monileur of Tuesday announces that the Commission of the Four Powers signed, on the 5th instant, at Constantinople, the final act of the rectification ot the Russian frontier in Asia. Some interesting details have been received from St. Petersburg relative to the reform in contemplation by the Czar in the situation of the serfs. These reforms will, it is said, consist, first, of the right accorded to the serfs to marry without the consent of their master, or not to marry, even though he should order them to do so ; secondly, corporal punishments caw no longer be inflicted, except on the sentence of a communal tribunal ; thirdly, the master cannot, at his own will, take the peasant from the plough to make him a servant, or assign him any other employment ; and fourthly, the peasant can no longer be transferred from one village to another. These are very material ameliorations, and will be accepted as an immense benefit by those who are the objects of them. A St. Petersburg letter informs us that the official journal confirms tlio account already given that the relations of Russia aud China have become unfit 'D'lly, in consequence of the Government of Pekin having refused to receive the Russian Ambassador. It declares that not only has China violated existing treaties, but ahe has

carried her insolence so lar as to place herselt in opposition to the whole ot Europe. lhe article states that serious eveuts may he expected to take place in China, and its tetiour indicates that Russia will not remain a passive spectator of what is going on.

SPAIN. According to the latest advices the Spanish Ministry is likely to have a good majority on the opening of the Cortes in January. The Queen has exercised conciliatory influence. The Duke and Duchess de Montpensier caused 12,000 reals to be distributed among charitable associations at Seville on occasion of the birth of the Prince. The Countess de Buena Esperanza, says the Epuca, is to be appointed principal attendant to the Royal child. Among the personages of distinction whose name figure in the register of the Prince's birth, as present when the Royal child was brought from the Queen's chamber, are the Duchess Dowager de Berwick y de Alba (mother of the Duke de Alba, who is married to the sister of the Empress of the French), and the Countess de Montijo (mother of tho Empress), both ladies of the Queen's chamber.

The Gazette publishes numerous addresses of congratulation to the Queen, one of them from the Spanish Embassy at Paris. COMMUNICATION. 'I'o the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, In the St. Croix Avis No. 87 þÿ 30th October last year is inserted a letter from G. J. Mudie Esq., in which is mentioned a deeisioft in case No 227 18.77 (of which copy annexed) concerning a complaint lodged by Mr. G J. Mudie against Mr. Henry Knight, which latter party was complained of as having apparently bought passes from some of Mr. Mudie's labourers. In the above-mentioned letter Mr. Mudie states us his opinion, that the decision would almost imply, "that a planter is legally entitled to purchase passes for as much money as he thinks proper, on condition he pays the money on or after the 1st October." 1 1 was considered at the time, that no notice need be taken by Mr. Knight of the aspersion, which seemed contained in the above remark of Mr. Mudie's, as the proceedings in the police court, inserted in connexion with it, did show clearly enough the groundlessness of Mr Mudie's opinion, the decision not entering into the merits of the case, but only throwing it out of court, the judge not considering it a public suit. As in the mean time the case has in one of the last newspapers, been mentioned as a case of bribery or the like in connexion with another alledged case of bribery, it has been thought proper in vindication of Mr. Knight's conduct to insert copy of proceedings in Erederiksted police court No 267 containing court of inqui- " ry whether planter II. ( From the Weekly Despatch, Dec. 13. ; THE KING OF DELHI. From the Calcutta Correspondent of the Times I have just received certain information as to the fate of the King of Delhi. His life is to be spared ; for the officer who arviolation of orders, gave him a pledge to that effect. The blunder is disastrous in the extreme. The hoary scoundrel deliberately ordered the murder of 48 English women and children, and his exemption from punishment will be interpreted by every native into fear. They will only laugh at the story of the pledge as an invention to conceal the inability of the Government to carry out its will. It seems, indeed, somewhat Quixotic to say that a police officer can save a murderer by promising him life. You must remember the king is only a simple subject. | He is protected by no treaty, and is in no sense a prisoner of war. The Court of Directors 50 years ago exempted his palace from the authority of the Courts of Justice, but only by an order, not by a treaty or agreement. He ought to be transported for life. As it is, he has played a winning game. If he had succeeded he would have gained an empire; as he has failed he loses simply nothing þÿ a perpetual encouragement to every native scoundrel with a few provinces and an army of ragamuffins

(From the Calcutta Correspondent of the Dally News.) Calcutta, Nov. 1. Every eye is still bent on Lucknow, for never was our position there more critical. It now appears that although General Havelock succeeded in relieving the garrison of Lucknow, it was at an enormous sacrifice of life, 26 officers and 200 men killed and 39 and 700 wounded. Still he succeeded, and earned the credit of saving our countrymen and women from death. No sooner, however, was their safety apparently secured than he was himself besieged. He is now occupying the position so long held by our garrison, but of his whole force there are barely 700 fit for duty, while the attacking force numbers thousands, and is daily being reinforced by the baffled garrison of Delhi. These latter, although worsted in every encounter with our troops, are creeping gradually into Oude, determined to make their last and fiercest stand in the land of their birth. Still there is no fear for Havelock so long as his provisions last, and these are in sufficient abundance to last till the 10th inst. Before that date can come round, in all human probability a force numbering from 4,000 to 5,000 Europeans, under the personal command of Sir Colin Campbell, will have at least attempted to extricate him from his position. Colonel Greathed's column, which was especially strong in cavalry, after all but destroying the Indore and Neemuch rebels at Agra, had marched on to Cawnpoor. It arrived at the latter station on the morning of the 26th, and expected to march into Oude next day, taking with them the 23rd Fusiliers, and

other detachments which were daily arriving there. Intelligence, however, reached Government that the Gwalior mutineers, no longer restrained by the Maharajah, were at ivalpec, and were inarching with all haste on Cawnpoor, taking a siege-train with them. This intelligence apparently decided the movements of the Commanderin-Chief. He sent orders, it is believed, to Colonel Greathed to remain at Cawnpoor, await his arrival there, and act, if necessary, against the Gwalior rebels; lie himself started the following evening (the 27th) iu a dawk carriage, and has before this, in all probability, reached Benares. General Garrett has been left to act for him during his absence, in the way of dispatching regiments up country, providing employment for the many officers of the Company's army who arrive in this country and find themselves without regiments. It is fortunate that all of the fugitives are making for Oude, for there they must stand at bay; there is no outlet for them; there they must fight, and there they will die. To the north is Nepaul entrenched against them by natural obstacles, and defended by its hardy population. .Sir Coliu Campbell will advance from the south, whilst a force, composed of the 10th Foot, Ghoorkas, au< Madras Sepoys, will guard the eastern outlets of Juanpoor, Azitngurh, and Gooukhpoor. Another force, advancing from the westward, through Rohilcund, will prevent any egress by that route. The great object is to save Havelock's force. That must be accomplished

at all risks. Meanwhile, troops are arrivi ing more quickly even than was antij cipated. Every day announces some lresh arrival. As they come in, they are hurried oft" with the most commendable dispatch, at the rate of about a hundred per diem. In another month there will be a very large force at Cawnpoor, or, it is to be hoped, at Lucknow itself.

SWEDEN. A private letter from Stockholm of the 30th ult., mentions that the financial crisis is severely felt there, and keeps the public mind in a state of much uneasiness. It is not, however, so absorbing as to exclude all interest on other topics, and the one which claims its share of attention is the letter of Count Henning Hamilton, Marshal of the Swedish Diet. The four orders of the Legislature þÿ the nobles, clergy, bourgeois, and peasants þÿ have each a President, but the person who (ills that post in the Assembly of Nobles is termed its Marshal. Some few weeks ago the Paris Steele published a letter purporting to be written by the Count and signed with his name, defending the intolerant views taken of religious matters by the majority of the Diet. That letter excited some attention in Paris, and produced in Stockholm considerable sensation. Count Hamilton has published a letter in the official journal of Stockholm repudiating, after a fashion, the authorship of the letter in the Sierle, while, at the same time, lie accuses one of his countrymen in Paris of an abuse of confidence. The repudiation, however, seems to be true only so far as his letter was a private communication addressed to a friend, and not to a newspaper. Count Hamilton does not deny having sent the documents on which the letter is founded, and those documents prove that he is, as stated in the epistolary shape, the adversary of religious liberty, the supporter of penal laws, and of banishment as

the penalty of a change of dogma. The Opposition journal, the Aftonbladet, of the 30th, notices the affair in severe terms. As Count Hamilton makes a very serious charge against some one, it declares that the Swedes resident in Paris (the number is very limited) " whether in high or low station," have an interest in repudiating in turn that accusation. Count Hamilton and M. Mauderstrom (the present Minister of Sweden in Paris), will enter the new Cabinet, which will he formed after the close of the Diet.

L CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 19th JANUARY, 1858. From the paucity of advertisements and political and domestic news, we have been obliged to follow the example of the American and some European Journals in devoting a portion of our columns to light literature in the shape of Romanci s &c. We commence to-day the pubiieutioi; uf a very (hulling Romancecalled" The War i rail," by Captain Mayne Reid It is a tale of Mexican Life and was expressly written for Chambers' Edinburgh Journal ; and furnished one of the most attractive features in that Journal during its publication.

We are sorry to learn that the appeal made by the British Consul at St Tnom.is to the British and other residents in this Island has not vet met with a willing response. The thai tol atrocities perpetrated on poor helple-s females a d children in India have aroused the just iiuiig nation of all Europe and America. A la. go n : in her of orphans and widows who call for syinp itiiy are daily arriving in England; and nations a e vie with each other in coining with aid to their assistance If nothing is done by us for them, wo are sure it will not he for tiie want of inclination, but the want of the moans.

(From the London Times.) It will gratify all but a very small section of the community to kuow that the exaction of proper amends for the Canton outrage is likely to he no longer delayed The course of action which wus recommended by our correspondent some months since, no doubt in accordance with thj providing opinion of the English on the spot, is about to be adopted. At the departure of the last mail it had been fully determined to seizo and hold Canton until reparation bad been made for the excesses of Ych and his satellites. It oertainly shows the spirit and resources of this country that in such an hour of national trial, with a vast army iu rovolt, and our Generals surrounded by tons of thousands of enemies in cue regit ni of Asia, wo are yet coolly preparing to attack the most populous seaport of the Chiuese Empire, and, if necessary, to carry the warfare up to the capital of its secluded and mysterious Sovereign. Though it is wonderful that the couitry should at such a time be able to spare troops at all, yet, as might be expected, the force which is to avengo our insults is far from largo. Even the full complement of sailors is not to bo had. The Shannon, which, with two or three other vossels, had furnished forth Captain Peel's Naval Brigade, was despatched from home for China service, and diverted under the pressure of the sternest necessity. Several steamers have also been sent to Calcutta, thus still further diminishing the forco available for any warlike achievement. But, on the other hand, some reinforcements had arrived, and our

countrymen, who do not seem to count odds, are disposed to make the best of what they have, and to commence operations at once. As a contrast to the doings of the sailing transports, we may call attention to the passage made by the Imperador, an auxiliary screw steamer, which arrived iu 70 days from England, bringing 500 Marine. The Imperador's passage to Singapore was only 6 1 days. The Imperadrix, a sister ship, was expected a few days later. This timely auecour teems to Have encouraged the

authorities to decide on immediate action. Within a short time it was hoped that the General in command would have from 2,000 to 3,000 soldiers and marines, and these, with the bluejackets, might be trusted to attack even Canton with its million of mob General Asbbumham had left for India, aud was succeeded by Go.ieral Siraubenzee, who had become highly popular, aud was looked upon as a commander of skill, activity, and daring. The gunboats were arriving daily, and, when united, were likely to play an important part in the series of operations. The hope that something would at last be done hud cheered men of every rank ; all were anxious for the signal to ascend the Canton River. The authorities had come to the same conclusion as the whole body of military and civilians þÿ namely, that it was better to treat the dispute as a local affair, and to deal with Canton as if its ruler had acted independently of the Imperial power. So the expedition of Lord Elgin to the Peiho, which had been delayed by his journey to Caloutta, was definitively abandoned, and diplomacy had determined to wait until the sword had done its work. This decision oertainly seems most wise. We have before dwelt upon the singular relations in which we find ourselves with respect to the Chinese people. The Celestials as a nation will not quarrel with us. Cauton is blockaded, but at all the other ports business goes on as briskly as ever. Shanghai aud Ningpo are, iu fact, thriving on the perversity of the s mtlitrn rabble Englishmen

are admitted freely into the country, penetrate into districts never before visited, asoend the Imperial Canal, gaze on the quays and boats, the temples and villas, and all the other wonders of this isolated civilization. They are received everywheie with a kind of merry curiosity, and even allowed by Mandarins and Custom-house officers to pass without payment of the usual dues It would certainly be as foolish as cruel to use any h irsh measures against this population merely on the theoretical grounds that the cenirai Government is responsible for the sots of its officials, and that the people must expiate the misdeeds of its Government A» it is, then, out of the question to do more than occupy as harmlessly as possible one or two points towards the North, and as it is moreover certain that such an occupation would be of no i fleet in bringing the Couit to reason, it follows that we must Strike the blow where it has been deserved, and wheie it is likely to produce the results we desire. It is the opinion of those on the spot that the seizure and occupation of Canton will obtain the re pa. a J ion which the dignity of the country requires, and also China tercoms.; between lead to a more permanent in- aud the civilized world. We must, therefore, wish every success to the bold measure on which the English commanders have decided. Indeed, the failure of a diplomatic mission to the Nortli might be predicted without mueh presumption. The very fact that we, who had alone been insulted and

injured, had called upon other nations to join us iu our remonstrances would be likely to encourage the Court of Pekin to obstinacy. Not only do we seem to show our weakness, but we who have a cause of war associate with ourselves other nations who have not a cause of war, and who therefore cannot legitimately carry matters to extremity. The natural conclusion that Chinese cunning must draw is, that we shall be hindred from any active proceedings by these entangling alliances. It is as well to show that this is not the case, and that England, by inviting other nations to share iu the advantages which will follow the opening of China, does not in any way cede her liberty of independent action. The plan of operations seems to be well considered. It embraces first the capture and occupation of Canton. We need not form any conjectures regarding the capacity of the English force for such an enter- Sirise orce has within the last few weeks achieved ; our numbers are small, but a smaller still greater exploits. The demands of the British Government ought certainly not to be merely nugatory. To take lasting possession of some advantageous spot near the great ports of the empire, ana command-

ing its main arteries, the Yangtse-Kiang, the Hoang-ho, and the Imperial Canal, ought to be the first well rities. We learn that the French have also determined to resort to hostilities against the Chinese. It is said that on some occasion a Ca-

tholic missionary has been murdered in China, and that France, considering her6olf the protectress of Catholic missions, resolves to punish the Chinese by force of arms. Baron Gros has with him a naval force from which he can land 600 leamen. He has therefore resolved to join in the operations against Canton. Thus we shall have the a ngular spectacle of two nations simultaneously prosecuting hostilities against the same people on different grounds, and without any formal convention of alliance. In fact, the two expeditions may be looked upon as entirely separate. The community which exists between the Plenipotentiaries can hardly be considered as extending to the military commanders. When England was injured and insulted by the Canton Governor she determined to despatch a force to the Chinese Seas to exact amends Believing that from these proceedings great changes might result, and seeing in prospect the opening of tho Chinese Empire and the immense increase of European trade, the Government of this country, in accordance with its policy 16 years since, desired to give to the chief nations of the world a share of the advantages that might accrue Accordingly, Prance anil America were invited to send Commissioners, and Russia has, qnite to our satisfaction, followed the example. at liberty to carry on war against the Chinese

Empire. The French mny invade it, occupy any p , ints on its territory, and exircise all the rights of war Similarly we, in prosecution of ou r just quarrel, must be considered as acting quite independently of any other Power. If French gunboats and French sailors attack Canton simultaneously with ourselves, it should ho understood beforehand that such a union is by no means analogous to the combined operations in the Crimea. In that ease there was a previous military convention, by which each of the allied Powers recognized its liabilities to the other, and bound itself to act in accordance with a common determination But here there has been no necessity for such a compact. Our forces are perfectly sufficient for the operations against China, and all th.it the interests of this country demand we shall carry out without dependence on foreign help. Thus, while we welcome tho co operation of our neighbours, we would guard against tho interpretation that there is any plan of combined military proceedings, or that either Power will have the right to limit in any way the action of the other, it is so far satisfactory that the justice of our cause is acknowledged by one of the most powerful European nations, associating itself with us in our first operations on the coast. Let us hope that the first will also be the last, and that the capture of Canton will he followed by such concessions on the part of the Chinese as will give to all civilized nations the liberties which they may in reason

demand. It is, however, as well to prepare for a more disagreeable alternative. A violent proclamation has been lately issued in the northern provinces, and it is quite possible that tho Court may think less of the recovery of Canton than of tho preservation of its own exclusiveness. When Canton has been taken it appears we can do but little for a time ; hut, should the Emperor n it grant that free en ry into tb t country which must he made an indi pensahle condition in an arrangement, there will he nothing for it but to send sufficient troops from India to compel acquiescence. But in this wo are looking too far into the. future Suffice it to say that, with our great European array iu the East, our noble fleet of transports, and vast resources for tho recruiting of Asiatic levies, there is no reason why we should not ca ry matters through with a strong hand. If this country lets slip the opportunity which it alone has the power to improve, the civilized world may he debarred for many a year front I roe communication w ith a third of the human race.

How to Save a Leaky Ship from Sinking, The attention of many practical men in this community has recently been drawn to a consideration of the best means of providing against or averting the foundering ot a ship at sea, and quite a number of suggestions have been thrown out through the press. The object is one of the deepest importance, and anything that promises a greater degree of safety than is now had must prove valuable In connection with this subject, we were waited on yesterday by a French gentleman, whose name we arc not at liberty to disclose, and placed in the possession of the following particulars : þÿ Some time ago, a slaver named The Three Friends, while making a trip from the coast, of Africa to Bahia, in Brazil, with three hundred negroes on board, was seen and chased by an English frigate. Finding the frigate overhauling her, the captain of The Three Friends came up with the lanyards of his standing rigging, which was then thrapped in to the mast, a short distance from the mast heads, the wedges were slackened around the mast, the main rail and plankshear sawed through about one-third their thickness, and other measures adopted to make the vessel increase lier speed. The sea was heavy, and she plunged through it at such a rate that she sprang a veiy serious leak, making nearly three feet of water an hour. All hands were employed in pumping and hailing, but the leak gained fast on them, despite their utmost efforts, and destruction

or capture stared them in the face. At this juncture the captain bethought him of the syphon and a large one was immediately prepared. A hole was cut through the stern of The Three Friends, just above the level of the water outside, the syphon inserted, the air ex hausted by means of a pumping apparatus fixed in the outer orifice, and capable of being in stantly withdrawn, and the water from the inside of the vessel started through the syphon Our informant says that the experiment was completely successful, the syphon discharging the water as fast as it leaked in the vessel. For twelve successive days, during which time the chase was maintained, the syphon was in successful operation, until The Three Friends arrived safely at Bahia. Our informant adds that lie will engage to keep any vessel from sinking, in this manner, provided she does not leak more than three feet of water per hour þÿ Boston Paper.

From the Illustrated London News. MALLET'S 36-INCH MORTAR. The largest shell habitually used by the armies of Europe is 13 inches diameter, and weighs in flight ISO pounds: it holds f) pounds of powder, can he thrown at the very utmost 4700 yards horizontally, and penetrates about three feet into hard earth, and scarcely through an arch of three feet thick by its fall. Mr. Mallet's object in designing these enormous mortars is to enable a shell of a yard in diameter, weighing about a ton and a quarter and holding nearly 500 pounds weight of powder, to be thrown to the same, or to possibly a greater, distance. The great mine thus suddenly transferred into an enemy's works has been ascertained lo penetrate into compact earth more than sixteen feet, and no arched bomb-proof or casemate exists which can resist its crashing fall : while the explosion of so large a mass of powder in the buried shell is capable of" excavating a crater of about forfv feet in diameter by about twenty feci in depth, and levelling buildings and works for a radius forty times greater than that of a 13inch shell. To project such a shell (one of which was actually thrown on the DUh < frtobor last, at Woolwich, with 70 lb. of powdci to project it, upwards of a mile and a half), a mortar of corresponding magnitude, strength, and weight is required. The actual weight of each of the 36-inch mortars is about fifty-two tons : hut such a mass, or even one-half the weight, it made in one piece, it would he perfectly

impossible to transport with any certainty over the best roads, and not at all over rough country ; and even by sea would he ditlicult to ship, carry, or land. One of the peculiarities, then, of these mortars is that they are readily capable of being separated into several distinct segments or parts, the heaviest of which unit weighs about as much as two 13-inch mortars, and that these segments ran he easily put together in the battery, or any one damaged segment taken out and replaced on the spot with a similar one. These mortars are, with the exception of the part called the base, made wholly of wrought iron ; ttie chase (or barrel) and chamhto being formed upon a peculiar principle, by which the external and internal parts of the whole thickness of metal are strained alike, and will break, if þÿat all, at the same time This is not the case in any solid cast or forged mortar or gun, which bursts at the internal surface first, and then rends f rom that towards the outside.

TO WIVES. The first inquiry of a woman after marriage should be, þÿ How shall I continue the love I have inspired ? How shall I preserve j Do the heart I have won þÿ? 1. Endeavor to make your þÿhusband habitation alluring and delightful to him. Let ; it be to him a sanctuary to which his heart may always turn from the calamities of life. Make it a repose from his cares, a shelter from the world, a home not for his person only, but for his heart. He may meet with pleasure in other houses, but let him find pleasure in his own. Should he be dejected, soothe him ; should he be silent and thoughtful, do not heedlessly disturb him ; should he be studious, favor him with all practicable facilities ; or should he be
and by your sweetness, gentleness, and good

humor, urge him continually to think, though he may not say it, þÿ This woman is, indeed, a comfort to me : 1 cannot but love her, and requite such gentleness and affection as they þÿdeserve. 2. Invariably adorn yourself with delicacy and modesty. These, to a man of refinement, are attractions the most highly captivating ; while their opposites never fail to inspire disgust. Let the delicacy and modesty of the bride be always, in a great degree, supported by the wife. a. If it be possible, let your husband suppose you think him a good husband, and it will be a strong stimulus to his being so. As long as he thinks he possesses the reputation, he will take some pains to deserve it; but when he has once lost the name, lie will be apt to abandon the reality. 4. Cultivate and exhibit with the greatest care and constancy, cheerfulness, and good humor. They give beauty to the finest face ; and impart charms where charms are not. On the contrary, a gloomy, dissatisfied manner, is chilling and repulsive to his feelings; he will be very apt to seek elsewhere for those smiles and that cheerfulness which he finds not in his own house. 5. In the article of dress, study your husþÿband stastes. The opinion of others on this subject is of but very little consequence, if he approves. ti. Particularly shun what the world calls, in ridicule, þÿ curtain þÿlectures. When you shut your door at night, endeavor to shut out at the same moment all discord and contention, and look upon your chamber as a

retreat from the vexations of the world, a shelter sacred to peace and affection. How indecorous, offensive, and sinful it is for a woman to exercise authority over her husband, and to say, þÿ I will not have it so. It shall be as I þÿlike! But I trust the number of those who adopt this unbecoming and disgraceful manner is so small as to render it unnecessary for me to enlarge on the subject. 7. Be careful never to join in a jest and laugh against vour husband. Conceal his faults, and speak only of his merits. Shun every approach to extravagance. The want of economy has involved millions in misery. Be neat, tidy, orderly, methodical. Rise early, beakfast early, have a place for every thing, and every thing in its place. 8. Few things please a man more than seeing his wife notable and clever in the management of her household. A know ledge of cookery, as well as every other branch in house-keeping, is indispensable in a female, and a wife should always endeavor to support with applause the character of the lady and the housewife. Let it be the stage on empire 9. Let home be your which, in the varied þÿ your world. character of wife, mother, and of mistress, you strive to shine. In its sober, quiet scenes, let your heart cast its anchor þÿ let your feelings and pursuits all be centered. Leave to your husband the task of distinguishing himself by his valor or talents. you seek for fame at home, let your applause be that of your servants, your chils i dren, your husband, your God.

AUSTRIA. Letters from Berlin announce that it has been stated almost officially that Austria is quite prepared to modify her pretensions in regard to the navigation of the Danube. This has been communicated to the Prussian Cabinet, with an intimation that Austria is about to seud a full memorial on the subject to all the Powers, According to advices received from towns in the western part of the Carpathians, some shocks of earthquake were felt on the 15th and 16th instant In some places the gable-ends of the houses fell in, and in others the ceilings and floors were injured. At Sillein, on the river Wang, the lower classes at first thought some evil spirits were playing their tricks, hut, when, informed that the undulating movement was caused by an earthquake, they rushed out of their houses, and, half-naked as they were, passed the whole night in the streets. At Tlniratz St. Martou, which lies in the midst of the Carpathians, the first shock was so very violent that many persons could not refrain from uttering a loud cry. A report 44 just like a clap of þÿthunder, was heard, and tlmu a rattling noise. The houses shook, and the walls, which seemed to move to and fro, cracked.
